summary: This is a shared foundation file for a series of AI helper commands in zsh. It gets loaded first (thanks to the underscore prefix) and provides utility functions for communicating with Ollama, processing output, handling git diffs, collecting user input interactively, and dispatching commands through either a direct command-line interface or an interactive menu. Think of it as the plumbing that all the individual ai-* functions depend on.

explanations.18: This creates an empty associative array (like a hash map) called AI_COMMANDS that will be populated by individual ai-* functions to register themselves.
explanations.19: Similar to line 18, this creates an empty associative array for AI_PARAMS that tracks what kind of input each registered command needs.
explanations.28: This reads the OLLAMA_HOST environment variable if it exists, otherwise defaults to the standard Ollama port on localhost.
explanations.29: This attempts a quick 2-second HTTP request to check if Ollama is running; if it fails, the function bails out immediately.
explanations.39: This reads OLLAMA_MODEL from the environment or uses 'qwen3-coder:30b' as the fallback model to query.
explanations.49: The 'print -r --' syntax ensures the prompt is printed exactly as-is without interpreting escape sequences or special characters.
explanations.50: The '-Rs' flags tell jq to read raw input and slurp it all into a single string, which handles very long inputs better than passing them as command-line arguments.
explanations.69: This pattern check tests whether the text contains any markdown code fences (three backticks); if not, the entire text is returned untouched.
explanations.75: The AWK script toggles an 'inside' flag every time it sees a line that starts with backticks (the fence markers), and only prints lines while inside is true.
explanations.85: The loop checks for 'bat' first, then falls back to 'batcat' (Debian's renamed version), returning the first one that exists on the system.
explanations.98: The ':A' flag expands the path to its absolute form, so we can later strip the current directory prefix to make it relative.
explanations.107: The `[[ ]]` test returns the success/failure of the pattern match directly—returns 0 if the answer starts with y or Y, otherwise 1.
explanations.126: This sets a character limit for diffs; if the diff exceeds this, a structural summary is sent instead to avoid overwhelming the AI model.
explanations.143: The parentheses with double hash `(( ... ))` perform arithmetic evaluation, so this checks if the diff size is less than or equal to the max.
explanations.151: This assigns a multiline string that starts with git statistics, then adds a header explaining what follows.
explanations.158: The `[1,$max]` syntax slices the string from character 1 to character $max, truncating it to the limit.
explanations.172: This tries to run _ai_bat to get the bat command name; if successful, the preview variable is updated to use syntax highlighting.
explanations.176: If the 'fd' command exists (a faster alternative to find), it's used to list files; otherwise find is used as a fallback.
explanations.194: The bare `read n` reads from standard input into the variable n without any flags; it accepts whatever the user types.
explanations.238: The `${+AI_COMMANDS[$cmd]}` syntax checks whether the key exists in the associative array, returning true if it does.
explanations.250: The `${(ok)AI_COMMANDS}` syntax sorts the keys of the array alphabetically (the 'o' flag) and iterates over them.
explanations.269: The `${(s: :)...}` syntax splits the string on spaces, so if AI_PARAMS contains 'file language', it becomes two separate items to loop through.
